sources.title: Human History Map, research coverage inventory
sources.note: Project inventory checked locally: oghuz-turks is a state record with approximate dates, exactly one observed 900 to 1000 interval, one border file, no existing card, and missing content review.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, ḠOZZ
sources.note: Scholarly reference checked for the western Oghuz migration and Syr Darya/Aral setting; Ibn Fadlan’s 922 encounter; Yengi-kent; the Qiniq/Seljuk branch; gradual conversion; and the warning that groupings called Oghuz or Toquz Oghuz cannot be collapsed into one simple identity.

sources.title: UNESCO, History of Civilizations of Central Asia, volume IV, part 1, The Oghuz
sources.note: UNESCO scholarly history, printed pp. 66 to 73: formation and geography; Yengi-kent; clan and wing organization; yabghu, council, atabeg and khatun; social hierarchy; trade and campaigns; tax revolt, Seljuk rivalry and mid-eleventh-century collapse.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, JABḠUYA
sources.note: Scholarly reference checked for yabghu as an old Turkic title, late tenth-century Islamization near Transoxiana, Yengi-kent as the early eleventh-century seat, rivalry with the Seljuks, and the title’s later disappearance.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, JAND
sources.note: Scholarly reference checked for tenth-century Jand and nearby Oghuz towns on the lower Syr Darya, Muslim merchant colonies receiving steppe and forest products, and the town’s place in Seljuk conversion and rival-yabghu traditions.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Central Asia X: Economy before the Timurids
sources.note: Scholarly regional reference checked for Yangikent/Yengi-kent developing from a leader’s winter pasture into the Oghuz capital near lower Syr Darya exchange routes.

sources.title: NYU Press, Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Mission to the Volga, translated by James E. Montgomery
sources.note: University-press edition record checked for the scholarly English translation and the mission’s 921 to 922 route. The account is a primary eyewitness report by a Muslim envoy and must be attributed rather than treated as a population survey.

sources.title: Ahmad ibn Fadlan, Oghuz section of the Risala, Arabic transcription
sources.note: Primary Arabic text checked at the Oghuz section: mobile haircloth tents and consultation; hospitality exchanges; illness isolation and unequal treatment; burial objects; elite feasting and gifts; and the author’s culturally loaded complaints about washing.

sources.title: Library of Arabic Literature, glossary to al-Sirafi and Ibn Fadlan
sources.note: Scholarly glossary checked at PDF p. 9 for manuscript بير تنكرى, transliterated bīr tankrī and normalized Old Turkic bir täŋri, “one God”; discussion also cautions that Ibn Fadlan did not explicitly call an Oghuz drink qımız.

sources.title: Institute of World History, Russian Academy of Sciences, Diplomatic gifts to the Oguz ruling elite
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article abstract and Russian text checked for Ibn Fadlan’s gifts to Oghuz leaders, the prestige of Central Asian textiles and spices, sheep as valuable hospitality goods, and visible differences in elite wealth.

sources.title: University of Tübingen, DFG Project Dzhankent
sources.note: Official research-project reports checked for Dzhankent’s multi-period development, Oghuz political context, Northern Silk Road links, houses and hearths, quern, pottery, glass, coins, animal remains, inscribed eggs, slave-trade hypothesis and archaeology’s limits.

sources.title: Härke and Arzhantseva, Interfaces and Crossroads, Journal of Urban Archaeology 3
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article record and full text checked: Dzhankent was a fortified ninth to eleventh-century settlement with older occupation, Khwarazmian and local/nomadic links, and plausible roles as winter quarters and a transshipment point.

sources.title: Härke et al., On the interface of steppe and urban civilization
sources.note: Interdisciplinary excavation report checked at printed pp. 113 to 120 for the 16-hectare walled site, dense tenth-century housing, pre-Oghuz settlement, mixed pottery and imported glass, Arabic graffiti, coins, fish/grain evidence, and absence of a monumental capital plan.

sources.title: Margulan Readings 2021, Dzhankent household archaeology
sources.note: Institute of Archaeology proceedings checked at PDF pp. 126 to 130: rooms with raised sufa platforms, tandirs and central hearths; storage jars sunk into floors; a tiled washwater soakaway or tashnau; and ram-headed ceramic hearth supports. No latrine is identified.

sources.title: KazNU Journal of History, Classification of kitchen pots from Dzhankent
sources.note: Peer-reviewed ceramic study checked for hand-built and wheel-thrown cooking pots, a heterogeneous kitchen assemblage, links with southern Kazakhstan, and the authors’ warning that classification remains incomplete.

sources.title: Larson et al., Provisioning a Silk Road City, Archaeometry
sources.note: Peer-reviewed 2026 isotopic study checked for Dzhankent’s growth into a fortified Oghuz center; sixteen sampled sheep; different birth seasons and grazing/fodder strategies; and the cautious inference that staggered lambing extended access to milk and meat.

sources.title: Haruda et al., The earliest domestic cat on the Silk Road, Scientific Reports
sources.note: Peer-reviewed open-access study checked for an adult male domestic cat dated 775 to 940 at Dzhankent, multiple healed or healing injuries, tooth loss, a high-protein diet and restricted mobility; authors infer sustained human care, without naming the caregiver’s identity.

sources.title: Darmenov, Khassenova and Nazarov, Signet ring with an inscription Muhammad from Jankent
sources.note: Peer-reviewed article checked at printed pp. 512 to 516 for mixed Muslim and Turkic town populations, mud-brick houses and narrow streets, washwater drains, coins, glazed ware, Arabic ornament and a Muhammad signet; objects could arrive through trade, gifts or warfare.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World, Diwan Lughat al-Turk
sources.note: Official heritage record checked for Mahmud al-Kashgari’s eleventh-century Arabic-Turkic dictionary as evidence for Turkic language, society and geography after this card’s atlas period.

sources.title: UNESCO Memory of the World nomination, Diwan Lughat al-Turk
sources.note: Official UNESCO nomination checked at PDF pp. 1 to 4 for the Diwan’s eleventh-century linguistic and ethnographic value, sole surviving manuscript and its copying in 1266. It is later evidence, not a tenth-century schoolbook.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Court and Cosmos: The Great Age of the Seljuqs
sources.note: Museum publication checked for the Seljuqs’ Oghuz steppe origins and their eleventh-century rise into a far-reaching, culturally productive empire. Used only for broad continuity, not to project later Seljuk court culture backward.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Azerbaijan VIII: Azeri Turkish
sources.note: Scholarly linguistic reference checked for Azerbaijani within the Oghuz branch and for related Oghuz varieties. Linguistic continuity is kept separate from claims of simple biological descent.

proposedOverrides.name: Oghuz Turks
proposedOverrides.summary: A source-checked guide to the western Oghuz Yabghu world, with daily life, Dzhankent archaeology, writing, sanitation, continuity and an explicit warning that the imported polygon is badly overextended.

batchIdentityNotes.finding: Exact target is the missing approximate 900 to 1000 state record oghuz-turks. It is interpreted as the western Oghuz confederation/Yabghu polity centered on the lower Syr Darya, Aral and northern Caspian orbit, not a modern nation and not every group ever called Oghuz.

The sole world-900 polygon has one part, three rings and 595 positions, bbox 50.3267033 E to 116.9633696 E and 36.8050782 N to 59.8827281 N. Its reach toward Lake Baikal/eastern Mongolia is historically indefensible, so the card treats it only as a broken locator.

Exact point tests include Yengi-kent, lower Syr Darya, Ustyurt and Mangystau while excluding Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Gurganj, Kashgar, Balkh and Itil. Neighbor overlap is extreme and confirms that the polygon cannot represent exclusive control.

Related records khazars, karluks, samanid-empire, pechenegs, kimek-kipchak-khaganate, seljuk-empire, cuman-kipchak-confederation, oghuz, khwarazmian-dynasty and turkmenistan remain distinct; none is merged or assigned this card.
The 1000 endpoint is a project cutoff. The Yabghu polity continued into the eleventh century; this bundle uses transformation rather than dissolution and gives no false extinction year.
